findings.where: First screen, the nav: 'Profile', 'Articles and talks' and 'Blog'
findings.fault: The three nav links have three different labels, but all three go to the same place (#article, the article specimen). A visitor who picks 'Profile' to check who Mark is gets a blog post instead. The nav promises three sections that the page does not have.
findings.who_objects: Bank or agency staff who want to check Mark's background before writing to him. They pick 'Profile', land on an article, and conclude that the navigation cannot be trusted.

findings.where: Article specimen, the publication row 'Streamlining the PPP Process … Lecture · 23 April 2026' with its blue download icon and 'PDF'
findings.fault: The row shows a download arrow and 'PDF', which promises a file. The link actually goes to #article, so nothing downloads and the visitor stays on the same page. The download signifier is false.
findings.who_objects: A procurement reader who wants to take the lecture away to read or share it, which is the reason a PDF list exists. They click 'PDF' and get nothing.

findings.where: Article specimen, the numbers of the three-item list ('1.', '2.', '3.') in house blue; the palette table's 'blue … list numbers' row
findings.fault: The list numbers are set in the link blue. The page's own note says blue appears 'only where something can be clicked', and the house reserves the link colour for links. The numbers borrow that colour, so they look clickable and weaken blue as the cue for a link.
findings.who_objects: A reader of an article who learns that blue means 'click here', and then finds blue numbers that do nothing. Angélique also inherits a rule that contradicts itself whenever she adds a list.

findings.where: First screen, the lockup at top left: 'Mark M. Moseley', a divider, then the MMM Infra arches and wordmark
findings.fault: The name comes first in reading order, but it is set small and light. The reversed aqueduct mark beside it is about three times as tall and much heavier. At a squint the firm's mark wins, so the name does not lead.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose binding test is 'his name leads, with the logo beside it'. Also a first-time visitor, who reads a firm's logo before a person.

findings.where: First screen, the logo reversed to warm white on slate (the palette note: 'the mark and the wordmark reverse to warm white')
findings.fault: The logo appears in a white version that the brand sheet does not list. Its grey arches and blue wordmark have been recoloured to fit the slate ground. A version the client does not hold is made only with the client's agreement.
findings.who_objects: Mark, as owner of the logo. Nobody has asked him for a reversed version, and the brand rule bars recolouring the logo without his agreement.

findings.where: First screen, the photograph (desktop and phone); the 'Graded for the site' texture specimen
findings.fault: The purple backdrop has been keyed out to flat slate, so Mark appears as a cut-out head and shoulders pasted onto a plain colour field. The hard keyed edge around his hair and shoulders shows. The brief asks for a full-bleed photograph of him speaking, graded into the house colours. This treatment turns it into a cut-out sticker and loses the lectern and the room, the 'at work' that names the direction.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging v7 against its card ('a full-bleed photograph of Mark speaking, graded', 'real people in real light'). Also a visitor, who reads a keyed-out head on flat colour as a cheap montage, not as a refined advisor.

findings.where: First screen, as a whole; nothing near the action
findings.fault: No proof of standing appears anywhere on the first screen. No body is named, no newest talk or venue is given, no event is named on the photograph, and nothing says where his work has taken place. The only reason given to write is a general opinion and a one-line description.
findings.who_objects: Development bank staff, who hire against terms of reference. They need to see that he has done this kind of work for bodies like theirs, and in their region, before writing to a stranger.

findings.where: First screen, the 'Placeholder: Mark's photo …' caption at bottom left (desktop)
findings.fault: The photograph's caption sits at the far left, under the text column, about 400 px from the photograph on the right. By proximity it reads as a footnote to the heading and the action, not as the photograph's label.
findings.who_objects: The founder judging the first screen. The note looks attached to the wrong thing, and it puts loose small print beside the one action.

findings.where: Article specimen, the publication row's title 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' and its 'Lecture · 23 April 2026' line
findings.fault: The row's title and date are indented a few pixels inside the text column's left edge. Every heading, paragraph, caption and list number above them aligns to that edge, so the row looks slightly off.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader of the article page. The page's own claim of a strict rhythm makes the slip easy to see.
